title: Escalate hyperkalemia with ECG changes
stem: A client with acute kidney injury has potassium 6.8 mmol/L, reference 3.5–5.0, and new ECG changes. What is the priority?
options: Activate urgent treatment and cardiac monitoring under protocol
Repeat the laboratory test before communicating the ECG change
Review the diet before requesting acute treatment
Assess muscle strength as the sole indicator of severity
why: Hyperkalemia with electrical changes can cause a life-threatening dysrhythmia.
Confirmation must not delay response to a dangerous clinical-laboratory pattern.
Dietary intake matters later but does not address the immediate cardiac threat.
Cardiac instability can occur regardless of the degree of weakness.
takeaway: Hyperkalemia with electrical changes can cause a life-threatening dysrhythmia.
learningObjective: Prioritize cardiac protection and protocol treatment when severe hyperkalemia has electrical effects.

title: Review a hemolyzed potassium result
stem: A stable client's unexpectedly high potassium result is flagged as heavily hemolyzed. There are no new symptoms or ECG changes. What is appropriate?
options: Leave verification until the next scheduled weekly blood draw
Promptly report and arrange an uncontaminated repeat per protocol
Document that the potassium is normal because the sample is hemolyzed
Administer a corrective dose independently based on the single result
why: A potentially critical result requires a prompt confirmation plan.
Hemolysis can falsely raise potassium, but the result still needs timely resolution.
Hemolysis makes interpretation uncertain rather than proving a normal value.
Unverified treatment can cause harm if the elevation is spurious.
takeaway: Hemolysis can falsely raise potassium, but the result still needs timely resolution.
learningObjective: Resolve a potentially spurious potassium result without dismissing a critical value.

title: Interpret hypokalemia with neuromuscular changes
stem: A client with prolonged vomiting has potassium 2.7 mmol/L, reference 3.5–5.0, weakness and reduced bowel activity. Which concerns should be included in the report? Select all that apply.
options: Oral intake alone will immediately correct the deficit
Risk of cardiac rhythm disturbance
Impaired muscle and gastrointestinal function
The potassium is reassuring because there is no chest pain
Reduced bowel activity confirms a mechanical obstruction
why: The severity and clinical context require an authorized replacement and monitoring plan.
Marked potassium depletion can disrupt cardiac electrical activity.
Potassium depletion can contribute to weakness and bowel hypomotility.
Dysrhythmia risk does not require chest pain.
Electrolyte-related ileus is a possible explanation and needs assessment.
takeaway: Marked potassium depletion can disrupt cardiac electrical activity.
learningObjective: Connect marked potassium depletion with weakness, bowel slowing and rhythm risk.

title: Recognize symptomatic hypocalcemia after neck surgery
stem: After thyroid surgery, a client develops tingling around the mouth and hand spasms. Which action is most appropriate?
options: Explain the symptoms as expected positioning soreness
Delay laboratory review until the next routine morning sample
Encourage rapid deep breathing to reduce anxiety
Assess airway symptoms and promptly report possible hypocalcemia
why: Perioral tingling and spasms suggest more than local postoperative discomfort.
New symptomatic calcium disturbance warrants earlier assessment.
Hyperventilation can worsen ionized-calcium-related symptoms.
Low calcium can cause tetany and may affect airway muscles.
takeaway: Low calcium can cause tetany and may affect airway muscles.
learningObjective: Escalate neuromuscular irritability suggesting low calcium after thyroid surgery.

title: Recognize concurrent magnesium depletion
stem: A client with prolonged gastrointestinal losses has low magnesium and persistent hypokalemia despite prescribed potassium replacement. What should the nurse communicate?
options: The magnesium deficit may be contributing to refractory hypokalemia
A normal sodium would rule out clinically important magnesium loss
The potassium order must have failed because replacement was unnecessary
The magnesium result can wait until all bowel symptoms resolve
why: Potassium correction can be difficult when magnesium depletion persists.
Different electrolyte abnormalities can occur independently.
Persistent depletion does not establish that potassium therapy was inappropriate.
Concurrent correction and monitoring may be needed during active illness.
takeaway: Potassium correction can be difficult when magnesium depletion persists.
learningObjective: Consider magnesium when potassium remains low despite prescribed replacement.

title: Respond to a seizure with severe hyponatremia
stem: A client with sodium 116 mmol/L, reference 135–145, develops a seizure. What is the priority after immediate airway and injury protection begins?
options: Wait for a second seizure to establish severity
Activate emergency treatment for symptomatic hyponatremia
Encourage salty food once the seizure stops as the complete plan
Give unrestricted water for thirst before the sodium plan is reviewed
why: The first seizure already demonstrates a serious symptomatic abnormality.
Seizure with marked sodium reduction requires urgent protocol-based management.
Diet alone is inadequate for this neurological emergency.
Additional free water can worsen the disturbance.
takeaway: Seizure with marked sodium reduction requires urgent protocol-based management.
learningObjective: Treat symptomatic severe sodium disturbance as an emergency requiring controlled correction.

title: Evaluate hypernatremia treatment safely
stem: A dehydrated older adult with marked hypernatremia receives a prescribed controlled fluid plan. Which observations are important? Select all that apply.
options: Intake, urine output and signs of fluid intolerance
Thirst relief alone proves the sodium is corrected
A faster infusion is needed whenever the client remains thirsty
A single improved value means further monitoring can stop
Serial sodium values and neurological findings
why: Replacement needs and tolerance change as treatment progresses.
Symptoms alone cannot measure serum sodium or correction rate.
Rate changes require the controlled plan and current assessment.
Continuing shifts and replacement still require trend assessment.
Both the correction trend and brain function help assess treatment safety.
takeaway: Both the correction trend and brain function help assess treatment safety.
learningObjective: Monitor neurological and fluid trends during prescribed controlled correction of hypernatremia.

title: Anticipate potassium changes during DKA treatment
stem: A client with diabetic ketoacidosis begins prescribed insulin and fluids. Initial potassium was high, but it is now falling. What explains the monitoring need?
options: The initial high result guarantees adequate potassium stores
Insulin causes potassium to remain exclusively in the blood
A falling value proves the glucose measurement is inaccurate
Insulin shifts potassium into cells while total stores may be depleted
why: Serum distribution does not reliably represent total body content during DKA.
Insulin generally promotes movement into cells.
Glucose and potassium can change together through the expected treatment mechanism.
A high initial serum value can mask a whole-body deficit.
takeaway: A high initial serum value can mask a whole-body deficit.
learningObjective: Explain why potassium may fall during insulin treatment despite an initially normal or high value.

title: Continue DKA care after glucose improves
stem: During DKA treatment, glucose approaches the protocol target but ketones and acidosis persist. What should the nurse anticipate?
options: Continued protocol insulin with prescribed glucose-containing fluid as indicated
Stopping the insulin solely because glucose has improved
Using urine colour as the main recovery criterion
Switching directly to routine meals without reviewing the protocol
why: Insulin may still be needed to clear ketosis while added glucose prevents hypoglycemia.
Stopping prematurely can leave ketoacidosis unresolved.
Urine appearance does not establish correction of acidosis or ketosis.
Transition depends on more than a single glucose target.
takeaway: Insulin may still be needed to clear ketosis while added glucose prevents hypoglycemia.
learningObjective: Distinguish improvement in glucose from resolution of ketoacidosis.

title: Recognize severe hyperosmolar illness without ketones
stem: An older adult with type 2 diabetes has very high glucose, profound dehydration and confusion, but few ketones. What is most consistent?
options: Normal age-related forgetfulness unrelated to physiology
A hyperosmolar emergency requiring urgent treatment
A mild illness because ketones are absent
A simple fasting effect requiring only a snack
why: Acute confusion with metabolic disturbance requires medical assessment.
Severe hyperglycemia and dehydration can cause dangerous hyperosmolality without marked ketosis.
Minimal ketosis does not make extreme hyperglycemia and confusion safe.
The glucose and dehydration pattern are inconsistent with uncomplicated fasting.
takeaway: Severe hyperglycemia and dehydration can cause dangerous hyperosmolality without marked ketosis.
learningObjective: Identify profound dehydration and neurological change as serious despite minimal ketosis.

title: Recognize diabetes insipidus after pituitary surgery
stem: After pituitary surgery, a client passes large amounts of very dilute urine and becomes increasingly thirsty; sodium rises above range. What is appropriate?
options: Record the urine as proof kidney function has fully recovered
Wait until the next daily weight before reviewing output
Promptly report possible diabetes insipidus and assess fluid balance
Restrict fluids because all postoperative patients retain water
why: The volume and dilution can indicate pathological water loss.
Rapid ongoing losses require earlier assessment.
Excess free-water loss after pituitary surgery can cause rapid dehydration and hypernatremia.
This pattern suggests water loss, and blanket restriction can worsen it.
takeaway: Excess free-water loss after pituitary surgery can cause rapid dehydration and hypernatremia.
learningObjective: Connect high dilute urine output and rising sodium with impaired antidiuretic function.

title: Apply a prescribed SIADH fluid limit
stem: A client with SIADH has a prescribed total daily fluid allowance. Which practices help implement it accurately? Select all that apply.
options: Coordinate the allowance across meals, medicines and shifts
Count only plain water because other drinks contain solute
Use thirst alone to decide when the allowance no longer applies
Apply a lower limit independently to speed correction
Include drinks, ice and other fluid sources identified in the plan
why: A shared plan prevents accidental excess and supports adherence.
Other beverages still contribute water to the fluid balance.
Thirst does not establish that the sodium disturbance has resolved.
Changing the prescribed plan can create avoidable treatment risks.
Uncounted sources can undermine the total prescribed allowance.
takeaway: Uncounted sources can undermine the total prescribed allowance.
learningObjective: Account for all fluid sources when carrying out an individualized SIADH restriction.

title: Recognize thyroid storm physiology
stem: A client with poorly controlled hyperthyroidism develops high fever, marked tachycardia, agitation and diarrhea during an infection. What is the priority?
options: Urgent assessment for thyroid storm and physiological support
Treat agitation as the only problem after checking orientation
Wait for the routine thyroid clinic appointment after infection resolves
Recommend exercise to reduce restlessness while awaiting results
why: The acute multisystem hypermetabolic pattern can become life-threatening.
Behavioural symptoms occur within a serious systemic pattern.
Infection can precipitate an acute endocrine emergency requiring immediate care.
Exertion adds demand during cardiovascular and metabolic instability.
takeaway: The acute multisystem hypermetabolic pattern can become life-threatening.
learningObjective: Escalate extreme hypermetabolic and neurological findings in a client with hyperthyroidism.

title: Recognize severe hypothyroid decompensation
stem: A client with untreated hypothyroidism becomes hypothermic, bradycardic and difficult to arouse with slow breathing. What is appropriate?
options: Wait for the client to wake before obtaining medical review
Activate emergency assessment and support ventilation under protocol
Focus on warming the hands before reassessing breathing
Attribute the slow pulse to improved relaxation
why: Impaired arousal is part of the emergency rather than a reason to delay.
Severe hypothyroid decompensation can compromise breathing, circulation and consciousness.
Peripheral comfort does not address the immediate ventilatory threat.
Bradycardia with hypothermia and reduced consciousness is not reassuring.
takeaway: Severe hypothyroid decompensation can compromise breathing, circulation and consciousness.
learningObjective: Identify hypothermia, reduced ventilation and altered consciousness as an endocrine emergency pattern.

title: Identify an adrenal-crisis pattern
stem: A client with known adrenal insufficiency has vomiting, profound weakness, hypotension, low sodium and high potassium. What should guide escalation?
options: A need to restrict every fluid source until pressure normalizes
A routine outpatient nutrition problem
Possible adrenal crisis requiring urgent replacement and circulation support
Simple fatigue from poor sleep alone
why: Hypotension may require prescribed resuscitation rather than blanket restriction.
The current physiological instability requires urgent management.
The history and combined clinical findings fit acute adrenal decompensation.
Fatigue does not explain shock and the electrolyte pattern.
takeaway: The history and combined clinical findings fit acute adrenal decompensation.
learningObjective: Integrate known adrenal insufficiency with hypotension and electrolyte findings during acute illness.

title: Assess sudden loss of catheter drainage
stem: A catheterized client develops suprapubic discomfort and no drainage after repositioning. Blood pressure is stable. What is the best first action?
options: Request an IV fluid bolus before checking the drainage system
Record acute kidney failure from the bag volume alone
Increase oral fluids and review at the next round
Inspect tubing position, kinks and drainage-system patency
why: More fluid does not correct an obstructed catheter.
The drainage pathway must be assessed before interpreting absent output.
Delay can prolong retention and discomfort if drainage is obstructed.
The timing and bladder discomfort suggest a potentially reversible mechanical obstruction.
takeaway: The timing and bladder discomfort suggest a potentially reversible mechanical obstruction.
learningObjective: Check reversible drainage obstruction before assuming all low output reflects renal failure.

title: Monitor after relief of urinary obstruction
stem: After urinary obstruction is relieved, a client passes unusually large volumes of urine for several hours. Which assessments are appropriate? Select all that apply.
options: Review ordered electrolyte measurements and the replacement plan
Assume the large output means no further renal monitoring is needed
Restrict all replacement because the client was previously retaining urine
Use urine clarity as the only evidence of recovery
Track output, blood pressure and symptoms of volume loss
why: Large losses may require carefully guided fluid and electrolyte replacement.
High output can coexist with ongoing recovery and dangerous losses.
Past retention does not determine current replacement needs.
Clear urine does not establish safe fluid balance or electrolyte status.
Post-obstructive diuresis can deplete circulating volume.
takeaway: Post-obstructive diuresis can deplete circulating volume.
learningObjective: Recognize fluid and electrolyte risks when marked diuresis follows obstruction relief.

title: Recognize possible dialysis-associated peritonitis
stem: A client receiving peritoneal dialysis has new abdominal pain and cloudy effluent. What is most appropriate?
options: Give routine constipation advice without assessing the dialysis findings
Promptly notify the dialysis team and follow the specimen protocol
Discard the effluent before discussing the appearance
Treat cloudiness as normal after every dwell
why: Constipation alone does not adequately explain this potential infectious complication.
The combination suggests peritonitis requiring timely investigation and treatment.
A diagnostic sample may be needed before further treatment.
A new cloudy appearance with pain should not be dismissed.
takeaway: The combination suggests peritonitis requiring timely investigation and treatment.
learningObjective: Escalate cloudy peritoneal effluent with abdominal symptoms while preserving aseptic sampling.

title: Report loss of fistula flow signs
stem: A client's established arteriovenous fistula had a palpable thrill yesterday. Today no thrill is detected after careful reassessment. What is appropriate?
options: Wait for the next dialysis session to mention the change
Apply a tight dressing to increase the pressure in the vessel
Promptly report possible loss of access patency
Use the fistula for a blood-pressure reading to test flow
why: Delay may reduce opportunities to preserve access.
External compression can further compromise flow.
A new absent thrill can indicate impaired flow or thrombosis.
Compression does not safely assess access function and may harm it.
takeaway: A new absent thrill can indicate impaired flow or thrombosis.
learningObjective: Recognize absent fistula vibration as a possible access problem requiring prompt review.

title: Escalate neurological change during initial dialysis
stem: During an initial hemodialysis session, a client develops increasing headache, vomiting and confusion. What should the assisting nurse do?
options: Treat the headache alone and continue routine observations
Assume confusion is expected because this is the first session
Postpone reporting until the full fluid-removal target is achieved
Alert the dialysis team immediately and support reassessment
why: Associated vomiting and confusion make isolated comfort treatment insufficient.
A first treatment does not make neurological deterioration normal.
Continuing toward a target without review may worsen instability.
Neurological symptoms during treatment may indicate a serious fluid or solute-shift complication.
takeaway: Neurological symptoms during treatment may indicate a serious fluid or solute-shift complication.
learningObjective: Recognize acute neurological symptoms during dialysis as requiring immediate treatment-team assessment.

title: Recognize a febrile stone complication
stem: A client with a known ureteric stone develops fever, chills and worsening flank pain despite analgesia. What is the priority?
options: Urgent assessment for infection with obstruction
Increase oral fluids as the complete plan to flush the stone
Wait to report until the stone is recovered in the strainer
Judge urgency only from the current pain score
why: An infected obstructed urinary system can deteriorate rapidly and may need drainage.
Fluids alone do not manage a potentially infected obstruction.
Passage is uncertain and infection needs current assessment.
Analgesia can lower pain without resolving infection or obstruction.
takeaway: An infected obstructed urinary system can deteriorate rapidly and may need drainage.
learningObjective: Escalate systemic infection cues in a client with possible urinary obstruction.

title: Recognize nephritic fluid consequences
stem: A young adult has cola-coloured urine, new facial puffiness, reduced urine output and hypertension after a recent infection. What concern should be reported?
options: A normal recovery response needing only reassurance
Possible acute glomerular disease with fluid retention
An isolated lower urinary infection based only on urine colour
Dehydration as the only explanation for dark urine
why: The new renal and hemodynamic findings are not routine convalescence.
The combined urinary, volume and pressure changes suggest renal involvement.
The edema, low output and hypertension require a broader renal assessment.
Dehydration alone does not explain the full retention pattern.
takeaway: The combined urinary, volume and pressure changes suggest renal involvement.
learningObjective: Connect hematuria with edema and hypertension to a possible acute renal process.

title: Monitor renal complications after rhabdomyolysis
stem: A client with confirmed rhabdomyolysis after a crush injury is receiving prescribed treatment. Which observations are particularly relevant? Select all that apply.
options: Normal temperature as proof kidney injury cannot occur
Urine output and renal-function trends
Potassium values and cardiac rhythm
Muscle pain improvement as the sole sign that risk has ended
Urine colour alone to determine whether prescribed fluids should stop
why: Rhabdomyolysis-associated kidney injury does not require fever.
Muscle breakdown products can contribute to acute kidney injury.
Released intracellular potassium can create dysrhythmia risk.
Less pain does not establish resolution of renal or electrolyte complications.
Colour is insufficient for individualized fluid and renal management.
takeaway: Muscle breakdown products can contribute to acute kidney injury.
learningObjective: Select kidney and electrolyte monitoring after major muscle injury.

title: Recognize losses during the diuretic recovery phase
stem: During recovery from acute kidney injury, urine output increases substantially while creatinine is still above baseline. What is appropriate?
options: Interpret high output as immediate return of normal renal function
Stop intake/output measurement once the first large void occurs
Resume all pre-illness drug doses without review
Continue close fluid and electrolyte monitoring
why: Urine quantity does not establish recovered concentrating or electrolyte control.
Ongoing losses need measurement to guide the recovery plan.
Drug clearance may remain altered despite improving urine output.
Recovering kidneys may excrete large volumes before normal regulation fully returns.
takeaway: Recovering kidneys may excrete large volumes before normal regulation fully returns.
learningObjective: Continue volume and electrolyte assessment when urine output rises during AKI recovery.

title: Monitor potassium after redistribution treatment
stem: A client with kidney failure receives protocol insulin and glucose for hyperkalemia. Potassium initially falls. Why are repeat potassium and glucose checks still needed?
options: The shift may be temporary and treatment can cause hypoglycemia
A lower potassium proves renal elimination has recovered
Only glucose needs follow-up once the rhythm improves
The initial glucose dose prevents every later low glucose
why: Insulin redistributes potassium without directly removing the body's excess.
The fall can occur through redistribution despite persistent kidney failure.
Potassium may rise again while elimination remains impaired.
Hypoglycemia can occur after treatment and requires monitoring.
takeaway: Insulin redistributes potassium without directly removing the body's excess.
learningObjective: Distinguish a temporary intracellular potassium shift from removal of excess body potassium.
